title: Transition to the endgame and the principle of two weaknesses
summary: Know the target endgame before you simplify, and win by stretching the defence between two weaknesses.

steps.md:
## Choosing the moment to simplify

A transition (exchange of queens or of the last pieces) changes the evaluation permanently. Before you exchange, **know the result of the target endgame**: pawn endings are calculated, rook endings with an extra pawn are often drawn, minor piece endings depend on structure.

**Rules:** exchange when the resulting ending is better for you than the middlegame; keep pieces when your advantage is dynamic (initiative, attack); when ahead in material, trade pieces, not pawns.

## Two weaknesses

One weakness can usually be defended. The winning method (Nimzowitsch, Shereshevsky): create a **second weakness** on the other side of the board, so the defender's pieces cannot cover both. Then **do not hurry**: improve every piece, use the king, and only then break through.

steps.prompt: White to move. A transition: one exchange decides the character of the ending (Alekhine-Capablanca, World Championship 1927)
steps.explain: **38.Bxe4!** dxe4 — Alekhine gives up the bishop pair to reach a queen ending where his queenside majority (a4 break) creates a passed pawn and Black's e4-pawn becomes a second weakness. Engine main line: 38.Bxe4 dxe4 39.a4 Kd8 40.axb5 axb5. (Alekhine-Capablanca, World Championship 1927; checked with Stockfish 19.)

steps.prompt: White to move. Black has weaknesses on a7 and c-file; add pressure on a second front (Kasparov-Karpov, World Championship 1985)
steps.explain: **25.Ra4!** — the rook attacks a7 and prepares to switch, tying Black down on the queenside before the king joins in the centre. Engine main line: 25.Ra4 b5 26.cxb5 Rb8 27.Ke3 Rdb6 28.Ra5 Bb7. (Kasparov-Karpov, World Championship 1985; checked with Stockfish 19.)

steps.prompt: White to move. Rubinstein converts by transforming the queenside (Rubinstein-Salwe, Lodz mt 1908)
steps.explain: **27.Rxc6!** — the exchange of the c6-pawn's defender opens the a-file and the c-file; after 27...Qxc6 28.Qxa7 White has a passed b-pawn, a second target on a6, and Black's d5-pawn remains weak. Engine main line: 27.Rxc6 Qxc6 28.Qxa7 Ra8 29.Qc5 Qe8 30.Bxa6 Qd8. (Rubinstein-Salwe, Lodz mt 1908; checked with Stockfish 19.)

steps.question: You are a pawn up in a position with queens and rooks. Your opponent offers a queen trade leading to a rook ending with 4 v 3 pawns on the same side. What do you know about that ending?
choices: It is usually a draw with correct defence, so keep the queens unless the ending has extra trumps
It is lost for the side with more pawns
It is always a win if you have the move
steps.explain: 4 v 3 on one side is the textbook drawn rook ending. Know the target result before you simplify.

steps.question: You have a weakness to attack on the queenside, but the opponent defends it with king and rook. What is the principle of two weaknesses telling you to do?
choices: Attack the queenside weakness with all pieces until it falls
Create a second target on the kingside (a pawn break, a passed pawn, an entry square) so that the defender cannot cover both
steps.explain: Defenders can hold one point. Stretching the defence across the board is how most "technical" endgames are won.

steps.prompt: Play this queenless middlegame as White (Kasparov-Karpov 1985, before 25.Ra4) against the engine (level 12). Attack the first weakness, create a second one, and do not hurry. Success = winning decisive material.

## Assignment

- **Puzzles**: 15 *endgame* puzzles where you must choose to exchange or not (theme *advantage*).
- **Guess the move**: Alekhine-Capablanca 1927 game 34 (in the corpus) from move 30 to the end — the textbook two-weaknesses technique.
- In Game review, find your last game where you exchanged queens: was the resulting endgame better for you than the middlegame?
